Title: krbtgt password is old
Finding: krbtgt password is older than 180 days in: contoso.com (400 days).
Risk: The krbtgt key signs every Kerberos ticket. If it was ever stolen, attackers can forge tickets (Golden Ticket) until it is changed twice.
Steps: Reset the krbtgt password twice, at least 10 hours apart (longer than the maximum ticket lifetime), using Microsoft's documented procedure or script. | Check replication between the two resets. | Repeat at least every 180 days.

Title: Privileged accounts have a service principal name (Kerberoastable)
Finding: 1 privileged account(s) have an SPN: contoso.com\svc.sql.
Risk: Any domain user can request a ticket for an account with an SPN and crack its password offline. If it is an admin, cracking it gives Tier 0 access.
Steps: Move the service to a group managed service account (gMSA) and remove the SPN from the admin account. | If the account must stay, give it a long random password (25+ characters) and remove it from privileged groups.

Title: Accounts do not require Kerberos pre-authentication (AS-REP roasting)
Finding: 1 account(s) don't require Kerberos pre-authentication: contoso.com\asrep.user.
Risk: Anyone can request encrypted data for these accounts without knowing the password, and crack it offline.
Steps: Remove "Do not require Kerberos preauthentication" from each account (Set-ADAccountControl -DoesNotRequirePreAuth $false).

Title: Unconstrained Kerberos delegation on non-DC accounts
Finding: 1 non-DC account(s) are trusted for unconstrained delegation: contoso.com\APP01.
Risk: A server trusted for unconstrained delegation stores the TGT of everyone who connects to it. Compromise of that server exposes those users, including admins.
Steps: Change each account to constrained or resource-based constrained delegation to the specific services it needs. | If delegation is not needed, turn it off.

Title: Computers run an unsupported Windows version
Finding: 2 computer(s) run an unsupported Windows version: contoso.com\WS02 (Windows 10), contoso.com\OLD01 (Windows Server 2012 R2).
Risk: Unsupported systems get no security fixes and are the easiest way in.
Steps: Upgrade or retire these computers; isolate any that must stay on a restricted network segment.

Title: Certificate templates let requesters choose the subject (possible ESC1)
Finding: 1 published certificate template(s) let the requester set the subject and can be used to sign in: VulnTemplate.
Risk: If low-privileged users can enroll, anyone can get a certificate that signs in as a domain admin.
Steps: Check enrollment permissions on each template listed. ADTD does not read ACLs. | Turn off "Supply in the request", or require CA manager approval, or remove authentication EKUs, or stop publishing the template.

Title: Seamless SSO key has not been rolled over for more than 30 days
Finding: AZUREADSSOACC key age: contoso.com 120 days.
Risk: The AZUREADSSOACC key lets anyone who steals it create Kerberos tickets that sign in as any synced user to Microsoft Entra ID.
Steps: Roll over the key with Update-AzureADSSOForest on the Entra Connect server (once per forest). | Schedule the rollover every 30 days. | Switch the account to AES after rolling the key.

Title: Domain controllers run an unsupported operating system
Finding: 1 domain controller(s) run an unsupported OS: EMEADC1 (Windows Server 2012 R2).
Risk: Out-of-support servers get no security updates. A domain controller holds every password hash in the domain, so one unpatched DC exposes the whole forest.
Steps: Build replacement domain controllers on Windows Server 2025 (or 2022) in the same sites. | Move any FSMO roles off the old DCs (Move-ADDirectoryServerOperationMasterRole). | Update DNS forwarders, DHCP options and hard-coded DC names that point at the old servers. | Demote the old DCs with Uninstall-ADDSDomainController and clean up their metadata. | Raise the domain and forest functional levels when the last old DC is gone.

Title: SYSVOL still replicates with FRS
Finding: SYSVOL uses FRS in: emea.contoso.com.
Risk: FRS is removed from Windows Server 2019 and later. You cannot add a newer domain controller to this domain until SYSVOL uses DFS Replication.
Steps: Check that all DCs replicate cleanly (repadmin /replsummary). | Run dfsrmig /setglobalstate 1, 2 and 3 in turn, waiting for every DC to reach each state (dfsrmig /getmigrationstate). | Confirm SYSVOL is shared from the SYSVOL_DFSR folder on every DC.

Title: A domain has only one writable domain controller
Finding: Only one writable DC in: emea.contoso.com.
Risk: If that server fails, the domain is down and must be restored from backup.
Steps: Add a second writable domain controller, preferably in a different site or host. | Make sure both are global catalogs and DNS servers. | Keep a tested system-state backup of at least one DC per domain.

Title: A site is not in any site link
Finding: Not in any site link: Auckland.
Risk: Domain controllers in that site cannot replicate with other sites.
Steps: Add the site to an IP site link (Active Directory Sites and Services > Inter-Site Transports > IP).

Title: Exchange servers are out of support
Finding: 1 Exchange server(s) out of support: EX2019 (Exchange 2019).
Risk: Unsupported Exchange servers get no security updates and are a common attack entry point.
Steps: Upgrade to Exchange Server Subscription Edition, or move mailboxes to Exchange Online. | If all mailboxes are in Exchange Online, keep only the Exchange Management Tools for recipient management and remove the last servers.

Title: External trust without SID filtering
Finding: External trusts without SID filtering: emea.contoso.com -> tailspin.local.
Risk: Without SID filtering an administrator in the trusted domain can add privileged SIDs to SID history and become an admin in your domain.
Steps: Turn quarantine back on: netdom trust <trusting> /domain:<trusted> /quarantine:yes. | Only leave it off during a migration that needs SID history, and turn it on afterwards.

Title: Too many accounts are domain or enterprise administrators
Finding: More than five enabled administrators: contoso.com Domain Admins: 8 enabled members.
Risk: Every Tier 0 account is a path to full control of the forest. Microsoft suggests fewer than five people with Domain Admins-equivalent access and no service accounts in Domain Admins.
Steps: List every member, including nested groups, and remove anyone who doesn't need permanent Tier 0 rights. | Delegate day-to-day tasks with scoped groups instead of Domain Admins. | Use separate admin accounts and privileged access workstations for Tier 0.

Title: Schema Admins or Enterprise Admins have permanent members
Finding: Schema/Enterprise Admins have 2 permanent member(s): Enterprise Admins: Administrator, Schema Admins: Administrator.
Risk: These groups are only needed for schema changes and forest-wide changes, and should normally be empty.
Steps: Remove all members, and add an account only for the duration of a planned change.

Title: Privileged accounts are not protected against delegation
Finding: 8 privileged account(s) are neither in Protected Users nor marked sensitive: contoso.com\svc.sql, contoso.com\da1, contoso.com\da2, contoso.com\da3, contoso.com\da4 and 3 more.
Risk: Admin accounts that are not marked "sensitive and cannot be delegated" (or in Protected Users) can be impersonated through Kerberos delegation.
Steps: Add human admin accounts to the Protected Users group (test first: it blocks NTLM, DES/RC4 and delegation for them). | For other privileged accounts, set "Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated".

Title: Privileged accounts with old or non-expiring passwords
Finding: 2 privileged account(s) have a password older than a year or set to never expire: contoso.com\Administrator, contoso.com\svc.sql.
Risk: Old admin passwords are more likely to have been exposed and reused.
Steps: Rotate the passwords of these accounts. | Remove "password never expires" from admin accounts, or better, use long passphrases with MFA-backed access (smart card, Windows Hello for Business).

Title: Privileged accounts are not being used
Finding: 1 enabled privileged account(s) have not signed in for 90 days: contoso.com\da.stale.
Risk: Enabled admin accounts that no one signs in with are an easy target nobody watches.
Steps: Disable these accounts, wait a few weeks for anything that breaks, then delete them.

Title: Operator groups have members
Finding: Operator groups have 1 member(s): contoso.com Account Operators: helpdesk1.
Risk: Account, Server, Backup and Print Operators can log on to DCs or edit privileged objects, so they are effectively Tier 0.
Steps: Empty these groups and delegate the specific tasks with scoped permissions instead.

Title: User accounts with service principal names (Kerberoastable)
Finding: 1 user account(s) have SPNs: contoso.com\svc.web.
Risk: Service accounts with SPNs can be attacked offline; weak or old passwords are cracked quickly.
Steps: Replace these accounts with group managed service accounts (gMSA), which have 120-character rotating passwords. | Where that is not possible, set passwords of 25+ random characters and enable AES encryption on the account.

Title: Accounts that do not need a password
Finding: 1 account(s) don't require a password: contoso.com\nopwd.user.
Risk: PASSWD_NOTREQD lets the account have an empty password.
Steps: Remove the flag (Set-ADUser -PasswordNotRequired $false) and set a password.

Title: Accounts limited to RC4 Kerberos encryption
Finding: 2 account(s) only allow RC4 for Kerberos: contoso.com\svc.web, contoso.com\AZUREADSSOACC.
Risk: Windows Server updates from July 2026 change the default Kerberos encryption type from RC4 to AES-256. Accounts limited to RC4 are easier to crack and may fail to authenticate.
Steps: Enable AES 128/256 on each account (msDS-SupportedEncryptionTypes = 0x18 or 0x1C during migration) and reset the password so AES keys exist. | For the AZUREADSSOACC account, roll over its key first, then switch it to AES.

Title: Accounts with SID history
Finding: 1 account(s) carry SID history: contoso.com\migrated.user.
Risk: SID history left after a migration can silently grant access, and is a known privilege-escalation technique.
Steps: After confirming resource ACLs have been re-permissioned, clear sIDHistory from migrated accounts.

Title: Any user can join computers to the domain (MachineAccountQuota)
Finding: MachineAccountQuota is above 0 in: contoso.com (10).
Risk: By default each user can create 10 computer accounts, which attackers use for relay and delegation attacks.
Steps: Set ms-DS-MachineAccountQuota to 0 on the domain. | Delegate "Create computer objects" on specific OUs to the people or tools that join devices.

Title: Default domain password policy is weak
Finding: Weak default password policy: contoso.com: minimum length 7, no lockout.
Risk: Short passwords and no lockout make password spraying easy.
Steps: Set a minimum length of at least 14 characters (fine-grained policies for admins can require more). | Set an account lockout threshold (for example 10 attempts) to slow down guessing. | Add Microsoft Entra Password Protection to block common and breached passwords on-premises.

Title: Some computers have no LAPS password
Finding: 80% of 5 Windows member computers have a LAPS password; 1 don't: contoso.com\WS02.
Risk: Computers without a managed password still share local admin credentials.
Steps: Check that the LAPS policy reaches these computers (event log Microsoft-Windows-LAPS/Operational). | Retire or fix computers that no longer apply policy.

Title: The Guest account is enabled
Finding: Guest is enabled in: contoso.com.
Risk: Guest allows unauthenticated-style access to resources shared with Everyone.
Steps: Disable the Guest account.

Title: Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access contains Anonymous or Everyone
Finding: Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access includes Anonymous or Everyone in: contoso.com.
Risk: Lets anonymous users read user and group information from the directory.
Steps: Remove Anonymous Logon and Everyone from the group; leave Authenticated Users only if old applications need it.

Title: Domain controller support ends within 12 months
Finding: 1 domain controller(s) reach end of support within 12 months: NYDC1 (Windows Server 2016, 2027-01-12).
Risk: Plan now so the replacement is finished before security updates stop.
Steps: Add Windows Server 2025 domain controllers to each affected site. | Transfer roles and demote the old DCs before the end-of-support date.

Title: Forest or domain functional level is below Windows Server 2016
Finding: Functional level below Windows Server 2016: Domain emea.contoso.com: Windows Server 2012 R2.
Risk: Lower levels block newer security features, such as privileged access management with time-bound group membership and automatic NTLM secret rolling for smart-card users.
Steps: Make sure every DC in the domain runs Windows Server 2016 or later. | Raise each domain level (Set-ADDomainMode), then the forest level (Set-ADForestMode).

Title: The Active Directory Recycle Bin is not enabled
Finding: The Active Directory Recycle Bin is not enabled.
Risk: Without it, restoring a deleted user, group or OU needs an authoritative restore from backup.
Steps: Run: Enable-ADOptionalFeature "Recycle Bin Feature" -Scope ForestOrConfigurationSet -Target <forest>. | It cannot be turned off, and objects deleted before it was enabled cannot be recovered with it.

Title: AD FS is (or was) deployed
Finding: AD FS configuration container found in: contoso.com.
Risk: AD FS adds servers to patch and protect as Tier 0, and makes cloud sign-in depend on on-premises availability. Microsoft recommends password hash sync for cloud authentication.
Steps: Inventory the relying parties in AD FS; move apps to Microsoft Entra ID enterprise apps. | Enable password hash sync and test with Staged Rollout. | Convert the federated domains to managed, then decommission AD FS and its DKM container.

Title: Users have non-routable UPN suffixes
Finding: 1 enabled user(s) have non-routable UPN suffixes: @contoso.local (1).
Risk: Users with UPNs such as user@contoso.local sync to Microsoft Entra ID as user@<tenant>.onmicrosoft.com, so their sign-in name differs from their email.
Steps: Add a routable UPN suffix that you have verified in Microsoft 365 (Active Directory Domains and Trusts > Properties > UPN Suffixes). | Change user UPNs to the new suffix (ideally matching their primary email). | Run IdFix to find other sync blockers.

Title: Enabled user accounts that have not signed in for 90 days
Finding: 2 enabled user account(s) have not signed in for 90 days: contoso.com\da.stale, contoso.com\old.user.
Risk: Unused accounts are rarely watched and are a common foothold.
Steps: Disable the accounts, move them to a quarantine OU, and delete them after your retention period. | Automate this with a lifecycle process or Microsoft Entra ID Governance.

Title: Enabled computer accounts that have not signed in for 90 days
Finding: 1 enabled computer account(s) have not signed in for 90 days: contoso.com\OLD01.
Risk: Stale computer accounts clutter the directory and can be reused by attackers.
Steps: Disable, then delete, computer accounts that no longer exist.

Title: User accounts with passwords that never expire
Finding: 3 user account(s) have passwords that never expire: contoso.com\Administrator, contoso.com\svc.sql, contoso.com\MSOL_1a2b3c4d5e6f.
Risk: Long-lived passwords are more likely to be leaked and reused. Microsoft no longer recommends forced periodic change for users with MFA, but "never expires" on shared or service accounts hides old passwords.
Steps: Review the list: convert service accounts to gMSA, and for people rely on MFA and banned-password checks instead of the flag.

Title: DnsAdmins has members
Finding: DnsAdmins has 1 member(s): contoso.com DnsAdmins: dns.op.
Risk: DnsAdmins members can load code on domain controllers running DNS.
Steps: Treat DnsAdmins as Tier 0: keep it empty or limited to Tier 0 admins.

Title: A site has no subnets
Finding: Sites without subnets: Auckland.
Risk: Clients never land in that site, so its domain controllers only serve clients by accident.
Steps: Assign the IP subnets of that location to the site, or delete the site if it is no longer used.

Title: A subnet is not assigned to a site
Finding: Subnets not assigned to a site: 192.168.99.0/24.
Risk: Clients in that subnet can pick any domain controller, including ones across slow WAN links.
Steps: Assign each subnet to the site of its location. | Check the Netlogon.log on DCs for NO_CLIENT_SITE entries to find subnets that are still missing.

Title: Manually created or disabled replication connections
Finding: 1 replication connection(s) are manual or disabled: DC02 -> NYDC1.
Risk: Manual connections are not maintained by the KCC and often outlive the reason they were created. Disabled connections can hide replication gaps.
Steps: Review each manual connection; delete it unless there is a documented reason, and let the KCC build the topology. | Check replication health with repadmin /replsummary and repadmin /showrepl.

Title: Microsoft Entra Connect Sync is in use
Finding: Microsoft Entra Connect Sync accounts found: contoso.com\MSOL_1a2b3c4d5e6f (server SYNC01).
Risk: Connect Sync is a full sync server that must be patched and protected as Tier 0. Microsoft is putting new sync features into Cloud Sync.
Steps: Keep Connect Sync on the latest version and protect the server as Tier 0. | Review the decision guide: move to Cloud Sync if you don't need device sync, advanced sync rules or more than 150,000 objects per domain.

Title: Enabled users without a UPN
Finding: 1 enabled user(s) have no UPN.
Risk: Accounts without a userPrincipalName sync with a generated name and are harder to manage.
Steps: Set a UPN on each account that will be synced.

Title: Microsoft Entra Kerberos (cloud Kerberos trust) is not set up
Finding: No AzureADKerberos object in: emea.contoso.com.
Risk: Cloud Kerberos trust is the recommended way to deploy Windows Hello for Business and FIDO2 security keys for on-premises access, without a PKI.
Steps: Create the Microsoft Entra Kerberos server object for each domain (Set-AzureADKerberosServer). | Enable Windows Hello for Business with "Use cloud trust for on-premises authentication".

Title: Microsoft Entra Password Protection is not deployed on domain controllers
Finding: No Microsoft Entra Password Protection DC agents are registered.
Risk: On-premises password changes aren't checked against the global banned password list.
Steps: Install the Password Protection proxy on member servers and the DC agent on every DC; start in audit mode, then enforce.
